title: Vapes: the soothers of the millennial generation
snippet: delayed adulthood and the yearning for utero
content_html:
Vapes are the soothers of the millennial generation. In a culture of melted futures and fizzling promises, all we have left are temporary pleasures. We lost our footing on the way to the dream life, and now, rung by rung, the ladder has been pulled away. But it still exists in phantom form—as the memory of a ladder. So we keep on climbing without making any progress, and blame ourselves for getting stuck in the same place.

We tell ourselves self-discipline must be the answer. If we could just pedal faster, or write better emails, or shave more time off our personal best, we will find the ladder again. It must be our fault we misplaced it. It must be our fault we can’t afford our own home. It must be our fault the cities we grew up in have become unaffordable. And the plastic in the ocean is killing the fish. Genocide, cultural erasure and cute dogs flow freely on our Instagram feeds. And to pacify us, we get to huff on a blue raspberry disposable vape that we bought in an unregulated phone repair shop that used to be an Xtravision.

Subscribe now

Our impulse to self-soothe in the wake of a world outside our control, feels like the moment you realise there’s a hurricane next door, and you shut the windows to have a wank. Taken in this way, vapes are a symbol of economic and political powerlessness. We have less means of controlling our own lives, but more objects to choose from to manage the stress. In the absence of agency, we get customer satisfaction, with more colours and flavours with cute little logos to trick us to think that we still make decisions. Our cup is empty, but we can still add more items to the basket and use Klarna at checkout. But puffing on a cartridge while the world goes up in smoke, is a bit like drowning on a sinking ship, but instead of being handed a life raft, we get colourful stickers of a life raft, as we continue to fall to our watery graves. So with the stickers, we still sink, but at least we get to sink in a cool, customisable way. Because we’re all individuals now. And we are important enough to know, that everyone drowns, the only choice left: is whether we get to drown and look hot while we’re choking.

Vapes are so deeply embedded in culture, that they have become taken for granted. And when something becomes so commonplace it seems unworthy of comment, that’s when it becomes ideology. Ideology lives in the everyday common sense, inside the pots and pans, the unrelenting glow of the screens we’ve lost our reflection in, disguising itself in plain sight, so visible that its hidden springs go undetected. In a society that is, in many ways—collapsing—rising levels of wealth inequality, higher grocery prices, mental breakdowns that go viral instead of getting treated with care—vapes have become a protection against structural despair. But we can’t solve structural despair with individual consumption. We can’t buy our way out of a housing crisis. We can’t push ourselves to the top of the queue for medication we needed last week. More smoke inhalation won’t lift stagnant wages, or make our loneliness disappear. A fresh drag of Watermelon Ice won’t prevent the bombs from dropping on innocent victims, illegal occupations on stolen land, or stop Big Tech from mining our data, but at least we can do cool smoke tricks now. So we French inhale while our future’s in freefall, and hold back the tears when the fumes get in our eyes.

Delayed adulthood is a term that gets bandied about a lot lately. And recently, I’ve seen examples of it everywhere. Last week, I was out in a pub in East London—a hipster-ish establishment that sold IPAs I’ve never heard of, to a clientele of creative directors and marketing teams, who were talking in accents they don’t have, about topics they don’t care about. (We all know you aren’t that passionate about queer representation, and that Eastenders lilt originated in Buckinghamshire..) Standing beside the bar, I spotted a quaint little wooden box full of crisps I hadn’t seen since childhood. It had all the greatest hits: Monster Munch, Hot Lips, Banshee Bones and Jonnie Onion Rings, and my excitement basking in the warm sentimental glow of the past, was soon overshadowed by the boiling horror beneath it: that we have no stakes in the future, but at least we can enjoy nostalgic snacks.

I had the same crushing realisation, when I met my agent at CAA. They have a massive boardroom corner office boasting a fridge fully stocked with Ribena (pre-mixed; in case we’re too hapless to dilute it ourselves.) In a culture where life becomes more uncertain, consumerism fulfils the role of a stand-in mother figure, coddling us into a comfort blanket, as she sings sweet lullabies to drown out the looming apocalypse. And faced with a crisis beyond our control, we crawl back into the womb. So our nostalgia for relics of a lost time, aren’t always in remembrance of the past, they’re often a yearning to return to a time before we were conscious. In utero, there were no responsibilities, or deadlines, or landlords, just sweet, unburdened bliss.

In the increasing instability of the present, the past has a closing down sale, and everything must go, but nothing is ever really allowed disappear. Whether it be vapes, Ribena or crisps that haven’t seen the light of day since the Iraq war; it’s always the same paint on a different wall—we are offered nostalgia instead of a better future, and coping mechanisms instead of political solutions. If you’re still living with your parents at the age of 36, that doesn’t make you a fuck up. Some of us flew the nest, and hit a brick wall, to stumble back with a clipped wing, and a feeling that life is passing us by. So if you’re a baby bird with a beard now, It’s not failure to launch when you can’t afford lunch.

The horizon of the good life has disappeared, and the promises that we’ve internalised have been uprooted. Unable to parse out this contradiction on the level of politics, we experience it as a personal flaw instead, so society’s failure becomes social anxiety. Compelled to either look inside at our own shortcomings, or look across at our neighbour’s nicer car. We can look anywhere we want, so long as we don’t look up.

Now, with nowhere left to dispose of our anger, we turn instead, to disposable vapes. But the grief still goes on, grazing skin that has become too hardened to feel it, oozing out of the crack in our smiles, and when we let the light in, we become translucent bodies, unable to hold onto hope as it slowly passes through. And while a nicotine rush might temporarily stifle the pangs from a stilted future, it can’t make us breathe easier, or believe that tomorrow will be better than yesterday. So when faced with the blinking red light, and staring down the barrel of an empty cartridge, we are confronted with a difficult truth: we vape, while we ourselves, are being vapourised.
